title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's idoneal numbers (numeri idonei). N is idoneal if every odd number represented in exactly one way as Nx^2+y^2 with gcd(Nx,y)=1 is a prime, a prime square, or a power of 2. Earlier in the paper he used the idoneal number 1848 to test 1848a^2+197^2 and tabulated primes up to 18,518,809 (a=100).

End of §76: the formula 1848a^2+197^2 is an 'inexhaustible source' for finding primes in the millions with modest effort. 197 can be replaced by other numbers, and other idoneal numbers can replace 1848. A larger idoneal number would reach larger primes. Euler reports that his search found no idoneal numbers beyond 1848 up to a stated bound, and that further ones are hardly probable.

Theorem: if N ≡ 2 (mod 4) is idoneal, then 4N is idoneal.

First proof (§77). A composite of the form Nx^2+y^2 below 9N can only use x=1 or x=2. If it had two representations N+a^2 = 4N+b^2, then a^2-b^2 = 3N ≡ 2 (mod 4), which is impossible, since a difference of two squares is never ≡ 2 mod 4. Likewise, take a number 4N+b^2 < 16N, i.e. the x=2 representation in Nx^2+y^2. Any second representation would have x=1 or x=3. These give differences 3N or 5N, both ≡ 2 mod 4, again impossible. So the representation is unique, and N idoneal forces the number to be prime. Hence all 4N+b^2 in (4N,16N) are prime, and 4N passes the criterion.

§78 checks this against the table of §34. The idoneal numbers ≡ 2 mod 4 are 2, 6, 10, 18, 22, 30, 42, 58, 70, 78, 102, 130, 190, 210, 330, 462. Their quadruples 8, ..., 1848 all appear in the table.

Second proof (§§79-80). Let N = 2i with i odd. Suppose a composite C = 2ia^2+b^2 = 2ic^2+d^2. Then b and d are odd, so d^2-b^2 ≡ 0 (mod 8). Since 2i is twice an odd number, 4 | a^2-c^2, so a and c have the same parity. Hence if C = 8if^2+b^2 (a = 2f), then c = 2g and C = 8ig^2+d^2 is a second representation. So uniquely represented numbers of the form 8ix^2+y^2 are prime, and 8i is idoneal (completed on p.50).
errors: No substantive mathematical error. Minor gaps: Euler does not spell out the primitivity/coprimality conditions (gcd(b,2N)=1, distinctness of the second representation) or the exceptional cases (prime squares, powers of 2) in the criterion. The first part of §77 (no composites up to 9N) is superfluous; the 4N-to-16N argument alone suffices.

The search bound stated here (transcribed as 7000) appears inconsistent with §81.6° on the next page, where Euler says he carried the computation to 4000 and then argues to 16000 only for numbers divisible by 4. Either the transcription misreads the numeral or the text is internally inconsistent.

ideas.what: Using a large idoneal number (1848) with a fixed y-value to generate large primes of the form 1848a^2+197^2
ideas.modern_name: Primality testing / certification via unique representation by quadratic forms whose discriminant has one class per genus
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1778 letters to Béguelin / papers E498, E708, E715, E719, E725)
ideas.where_published: E719 itself and related Nova Acta papers; discussed by Dickson History I ch. XIV, Weil 'Number Theory', Frei, Steinig

ideas.what: Belief, from computation, that 1848 is the largest idoneal number
ideas.modern_name: Finiteness of idoneal numbers (one class per genus); Chowla 1934, Weinberger 1973 (at most one more, none under GRH)

ideas.what: If N ≡ 2 mod 4 is idoneal then 4N is idoneal, proved by parity of differences of squares
ideas.modern_name: Genus/class number relation between discriminants -4n and -16n (conductor-2 orders); one of Euler's idoneal rules
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; rigorous treatment of Euler's idoneal theorems by Grube (1874)
ideas.where_published: E719 (this page); recounted in Dickson History vol. I and Grube 1874

ideas.what: Alternative proof: for N = 2i (i odd), any two representations 2ia^2+b^2 = 2ic^2+d^2 have a ≡ c mod 2, so idoneality passes to 8i
ideas.modern_name: Parity (2-adic) argument on representations; implies the 4N rule

deep.surprise_reason: The 4N rule for N ≡ 2 mod 4, the 1848-based prime table and the conjecture that 1848 is the last idoneal number are all well documented (Dickson, Grube, Weil, Weinberger). The proofs are neat but elementary and nothing here seems absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: 'etiam majores eum praecedentes' – image reads roughly 'etiam majores eum praecedentes'; the sense is 'numbers larger than the preceding ones'. The '[?]' is unnecessary but the wording is awkward.
The search bound 'usque ad terminum 7000' is hard to read in the scan; check it against §81.6° ('usque ad 4 millia').
§77: 'intra intervallum N et 4N formula Nxx+yy non nisi numeros primos praebebit' – correct; in the image '16N' is written with a correction mark over 'N'.
